quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what a spot design is and the six ways of arranging motifs on a ground.

questions.q: What is a spot design?
options: A stripe formed by two weaves across the ends
A cloth with two complete layers
A weave with ridges and hollows around a diamond
A small motif repeated at regular intervals on a plain or other ground
questions.explain: A spot design distributes a small motif at regular intervals over a ground weave. Stripes, double cloths and honeycombs are different structures altogether.

questions.q: How many methods of arranging spots does the lecture list?
questions.explain: The lecture lists six methods, labelled A to F: straight rows, alternate (half-drop) rows, twill base, sateen base, reversed in alternate positions and diamond (pointed) order.

questions.q: Which base does the lecture call the most useful for distributing spots?
questions.explain: The sateen base spreads the spots evenly with no obvious lines. Straight rows and a twill base both produce visible lines of spots.

questions.q: Arranging spots in alternate rows is also called a half-drop arrangement.
questions.explain: Method B places each row of spots half a repeat along from the row before, which is the half-drop order.

questions.q: In the lecture's example, what weave forms the ground between the spots?
questions.explain: The ground is plain weave; the 5-end sateen is only the base that decides where the spot centres fall, not a weave in the cloth.

questions.q: On the point paper in the lecture, what do the blue squares show?
questions.explain: Blue squares are the motif lifts and grey squares are the plain ground. Nothing on the design paper represents the reed.

questions.q: A spot arranged on a twill base will show the spots lying along a diagonal line.
questions.explain: A twill base moves each spot one step diagonally, so the spots line up on a visible diagonal, which is why the sateen base is preferred.

questions.q: What does the lecture mean by the 'reversed in alternate positions' method?
options: The spot is omitted in alternate repeats
Every second motif is turned over so it faces the other way
The ground weave is reversed under every spot
questions.explain: Method E reverses the motif in alternate positions so neighbouring spots mirror each other, giving a less mechanical look.

questions.q: Which arrangement places the spots in a pointed, zigzag order?
questions.explain: The diamond or pointed order steps the spots up and then back down like a pointed twill, forming a diamond lattice.

questions.q: The move number of a sateen base is the number of picks between one spot and the next in the same row.
questions.explain: The move number is the step in ends (or picks) from one sateen lift to the next; in the example a move of 2 on the 5-end base becomes 2 × 6 = 12 ends between successive spot centres, not a count of picks.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How intervals, move numbers and base weaves fix the size and spacing of a spot repeat.

questions.q: A spot design is built on a 5-end sateen base with an interval of 6 ends. How wide is the full repeat?
questions.explain: Repeat width = base ends × end interval = 5 × 6 = 30 ends. Adding 5 + 6 = 11 is a common slip.

questions.q: If the pick interval of a spot design is increased while the base and end interval stay the same, what happens?
options: More spots fit in each repeat
The spots move onto a twill line
The repeat becomes taller and the spots further apart pick-way
questions.explain: Repeat height = base picks × pick interval, so a larger pick interval stretches the repeat upward and spaces the spots further apart; the number of spots per repeat stays equal to the base size.

questions.q: How many spots are there in one repeat of a design laid on a 5-end sateen base, whatever the intervals?
questions.explain: A 5-end sateen has exactly five lifts per repeat, so it carries five spot centres. The intervals change spacing, not the count.

questions.q: In the lecture's example the spot centres in successive pick rows move 12 ends to the right because the base move number is 2 and the end interval is 6.
questions.explain: Each sateen step of 2 ends is scaled by the 6-end interval, so 2 × 6 = 12 ends; starting at end 4 the centres fall on ends 16, 28, 40 − 30 = 10 and 22.

questions.q: Which formula gives the number of ends between successive spot centres in the lecture's example?
questions.explain: Ends between centres = move number × end interval = 2 × 6 = 12. Base ends × interval (30) is the whole repeat, not the step.

questions.q: A spot design is placed on a plain ground. The motif begins on an end and pick that break the plain order. What is the result?
options: The spot is lost in the ground
The spots fall into straight rows
Long floats appear at the edges of the motif
questions.explain: The lecture's 'plain basis, alternate order' rule: the motif must start where it continues the plain interlacing, otherwise its edges leave long floats.

questions.q: With a fixed interval of 6 ends and 8 picks, which base gives the larger repeat?
options: It depends on the motif size
questions.explain: Repeat = base size × interval, so an 8-end base gives 48 × 64 against 30 × 40 for the 5-end base.

questions.q: Doubling both intervals of a sateen-based spot design doubles the number of spots per square inch of cloth.
questions.explain: Doubling both intervals makes the repeat four times the area while it still holds the same five spots, so spots per square inch fall to a quarter.

questions.q: How are spot-centre positions related to the sateen base?
options: The base decides the colour of each spot
The base fixes the number of healds
Each sateen lift is multiplied by the intervals to give the centre's end and pick
The base is woven as it stands and the spot sits inside each float
questions.explain: Each lift of the base weave is scaled: its end number by the end interval and its pick number by the pick interval, which places the spot centres.

questions.q: Why does the sateen base avoid visible lines of spots?
options: It uses more spots per repeat
Its lifts never fall on one straight or diagonal line
questions.explain: A sateen's lifts are distributed so that no two adjacent ones touch or lie on a continuous diagonal, so the spots look scattered.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work out repeat sizes, spot positions and spot densities from base weaves and intervals.

questions.q: A spot design uses a 5-end sateen base with intervals of 6 ends and 8 picks. How many picks are in one repeat?
questions.explain: Repeat picks = base picks × pick interval = 5 × 8 = 40.

questions.q: A 5-end sateen base with intervals of 6 ends and 8 picks gives a 30 × 40 repeat holding five spots. How many ends-and-picks squares of the repeat belong to each spot, on average?
questions.explain: Area of repeat = 30 × 40 = 1,200 squares; shared by five spots gives 1,200 ÷ 5 = 240 squares per spot.

questions.q: On a 5-end sateen base with a move number of 2 and an end interval of 6, the first spot centre is at end 4. On which end is the second centre?
questions.explain: Step = 2 × 6 = 12 ends, so the second centre is at end 4 + 12 = 16, matching the lecture's 4, 16, 28, 10, 22.

questions.q: Continuing the same design (30-end repeat, step of 12 ends), the third centre is at end 28. On which end does the fourth centre fall after wrapping round the repeat?
questions.explain: 28 + 12 = 40, which is beyond the 30-end repeat, so subtract 30: end 10.

questions.q: In the lecture's example the spot centres fall on picks 5, 13, 21, 29 and 37. What is the pick interval between successive centres?
questions.explain: Successive centres are 13 − 5 = 8 picks apart, the pick interval of the design.

questions.q: A spot design has a 30 × 40 repeat with five spots. The cloth is set at 60 ends per inch and 80 picks per inch. How many spots are there per square inch of cloth?
questions.explain: Repeats per inch: 60 ÷ 30 = 2 across and 80 ÷ 40 = 2 up, so 4 repeats per square inch × 5 spots = 20 spots.

questions.q: An 8-end sateen base is used with intervals of 5 ends and 7 picks. How many ends are in the full repeat?
questions.explain: Repeat ends = 8 × 5 = 40 ends (and 8 × 7 = 56 picks).

questions.q: A 5-end sateen base with a move number of 3 is used with an end interval of 4. How many ends apart are successive spot centres?
questions.explain: Step between centres = move number × end interval = 3 × 4 = 12 ends.

questions.q: A diamond motif on point paper lifts 1, 3, 5, 3 and 1 ends on its five picks. How many motif squares does one spot contain?
questions.explain: 1 + 3 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 13 motif lifts. Counting only the widest row (5) or the rows (5) is the usual error.

questions.q: A 30 × 40 spot repeat is woven at 60 ends per inch. How wide is one repeat in the cloth?
questions.explain: Width = 30 ends ÷ 60 ends per inch = 0.5 inch. Dividing the other way round gives 2, a common mistake.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Design-room decisions: choosing a base, placing a motif correctly and spotting what went wrong on the loom.

questions.q: A customer complains that the spots on a sample 'line up like soldiers' across the cloth. Which arrangement was most likely used, and what should you change to?
options: Straight rows; move to a sateen base
Sateen base; move to straight rows
Half-drop; move to a twill base
Diamond order; move to a twill base
questions.explain: Straight rows put every spot on a line. Redistributing the centres on a sateen base removes the obvious rows.

questions.q: The edges of a small motif on a plain ground show long, untidy floats in the woven sample. What was the likely mistake on point paper?
options: The motif was drawn in blue instead of grey
The motif was started on an end and pick that did not continue the plain order
The sateen base had too many ends
The pick interval was too large
questions.explain: The lecture's rule: on a plain basis the motif must start in the alternate order of the ground, or its edges leave floats.

questions.q: A designer wants spots further apart pick-way without changing the cloth sett or the number of spots per repeat. What should change?
questions.explain: The pick interval scales the vertical spacing of the centres; the base size would change the number of spots per repeat.

questions.q: A dobby can control a limited repeat of picks. Which spot design is easiest to weave on it?
options: 8-end sateen base, intervals 6 ends × 8 picks (64 picks)
5-end sateen base, intervals 6 ends × 16 picks (80 picks)
8-end sateen base, intervals 5 ends × 12 picks (96 picks)
5-end sateen base, intervals 6 ends × 8 picks (40 picks)
questions.explain: The repeat in picks is base picks × pick interval; 5 × 8 = 40 is the smallest and so needs the shortest peg plan.

questions.q: For a diamond (pointed) arrangement of spots the design will show the spots in a zigzag lattice rather than scattered.
questions.explain: The pointed order steps spots up and back down, forming a visible diamond lattice; it is chosen when that lattice is wanted.

questions.q: A sample shows the spots well scattered with no visible rows or diagonals. Which base was most probably used?
questions.explain: Only the sateen base gives the even, line-free scatter; twills and rows produce visible lines.

questions.q: A buyer asks for a lighter, more open spot design on the same plain ground. Which change gives fewer spots per square inch?
options: Change from a 5-end to an 8-end base with the same intervals, keeping repeat area per spot the same
questions.explain: Larger intervals enlarge the repeat while the number of spots per repeat stays fixed, so spots per square inch fall.

questions.q: Two spot designs have the same 30 × 40 repeat and five spots each; one is on a sateen base, the other on a twill base. Which is true?
options: Both have the same spot density but the twill version shows diagonal lines
The sateen version has more spots per repeat
The twill version consumes more yarn
The sateen version needs a larger loom
questions.explain: Density depends only on repeat size and spot count, which are equal; the distribution decides whether lines are visible.

questions.q: When drawing a spot design on point paper, which should be fixed first?
options: The base weave and its intervals, to locate the centres
questions.explain: The centres come from scaling the base weave by the intervals; the motif is then drawn round each centre, respecting the ground order.

questions.q: Reversing the motif in alternate positions (method E) changes the number of spots in the repeat.
questions.explain: Reversal only turns alternate motifs over; the count and spacing of spots are unchanged.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder two-step questions across the whole lecture, including the usual slips with repeats and bases.

questions.q: A spot design is on a 5-end sateen base with intervals of 6 ends and 8 picks, so its repeat is 30 × 40. The cloth is set at 72 ends per inch and 64 picks per inch. How many spots are there per square inch? Give two decimals.
questions.explain: Repeats per inch: 72 ÷ 30 = 2.4 across and 64 ÷ 40 = 1.6 up; 2.4 × 1.6 = 3.84 repeats × 5 spots = 19.2 spots per square inch.

questions.q: A design is on a 5-end sateen base, move number 2, end interval 6, first centre at end 4. Which list gives the five spot-centre ends in the order they occur pick by pick?
questions.explain: Each step adds 12 ends and wraps at 30: 4, 16, 28, 40 − 30 = 10, 22. Option B is sorted, not in pick order; option D forgets to wrap.

questions.q: A student doubles the end interval from 6 to 12 but keeps the pick interval at 8 on the 5-end base. What is the new repeat?
questions.explain: Only the end interval changed: 5 × 12 = 60 ends; picks stay 5 × 8 = 40.

questions.q: With a plain ground, a motif placed one end to the right of its correct position can still weave cleanly if it is also moved one pick up.
questions.explain: Plain weave alternates in both directions, so shifting one end and one pick lands back on the same interlacing order; shifting one end alone breaks it.

questions.q: A motif is 5 ends wide and 5 picks high. On a 30 × 40 repeat with five spots, what fraction of the repeat area is covered by motifs? Give the answer as a percentage to one decimal.
Which pair correctly matches a method with its typical appearance?
options: Twill base – spots on a diagonal line; sateen base – spots evenly scattered
Twill base – spots scattered; sateen base – spots on a diagonal
Straight rows – spots scattered; half-drop – spots in columns
Diamond order – spots in straight rows; straight rows – diamond lattice
questions.explain: The twill base follows a diagonal, the sateen base scatters the lifts; the other pairings swap the effects.

questions.q: A 30 × 40 spot repeat is woven at 60 ends and 80 picks per inch. How many complete repeats fit across a 45-inch cloth width?
questions.explain: Ends in the width = 45 × 60 = 2,700; divided by 30 ends per repeat = 90 repeats.

questions.q: Why does the lecture keep the ground plain even though the spot centres come from a sateen?
options: Plain weave has the same repeat as sateen
Plain weave needs fewer picks per inch
The sateen only locates the centres; a plain ground is firm and shows the motif clearly
Sateen cannot be drawn on point paper
questions.explain: The base weave is a distribution tool, not a cloth structure; the ground can be plain or another weave, and plain is the simplest firm ground.

questions.q: On a 5-end sateen base the five spots occupy five different pick rows. On which rows do the centres lie if the pick interval is 8 and the first centre is on pick 5?
questions.explain: Each successive sateen row is one pick interval higher: 5, 13, 21, 29, 37. Option D lists the same picks but not in row order.

questions.q: The grey squares on the lecture's point paper are lifts that belong to the sateen base weave.
questions.explain: Grey squares are the plain-ground lifts; the sateen base is not woven at all, it only fixes where the blue motif lifts are centred.
